Atom and Its Structure

Atoms

  • Atoms are the smallest component of an element and are building blocks of matter. An atom is composed of protons (p), neutrons (n) and electrons (e⁻).

LAWS OF CHEMICAL COMBINATION

Law of Conservation of Mass

  • The law of Conservation of Mass states that in a closed system, the total mass of a system remains constant over time, meaning mass is neither created nor destroyed, but can only change form.
  • This was given by Antoine Lavoisier.

Law of Constant Proportion

  • The law states that a given chemical compound always contains its component elements in a fixed ratio by mass, regardless of its source or method of preparation.
  • This was given by Joseph Proust.

Dalton's Atomic Theory (1808)

According to Dalton's Theory:

  • All matter is made of indivisible particles called atoms, which cannot be created nor destroyed.
  • Atoms of the same element have identical mass and physical properties.
  • Compounds are combinations of atoms of two or more elements.
  • All chemical reactions involve the rearrangement of atoms.

THE ATOMIC MODELS

J. J. Thomson and Discovery of Electron (1897)

1897: J. J. Thomson performed Cathode-Ray Experiment by observing streams of particles emitted by cathode of a vacuum tube, which led to the discovery the electron.

He proposed:

  • (i) An atom consists of a positively charged sphere and the electrons are embedded in it.
  • (ii) The negative and positive charges are equal in magnitude. So, the atom as a whole is electrically neutral.
  • 1904: J. J. Thomson proposed the first atomic model, often referred to as the "Plum Pudding Model", "Raisin Pudding Model", or "Watermelon Model". In this model, the positive charge is spread throughout the atom (like the bulk of pudding or watermelon), while the electrons are embedded within it (like plums or seeds).

Ernest Rutherford's Atomic Model (1911)

  • In 1909, Ernest Rutherford conducted the Gold Foil Experiment with the help of Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden.

Gold Foil Experiment Findings

  • A few α-particle were deflected at small and large angles, indicating the presence of a dense, positively charged nucleus.
  • Rutherford used gold foil (about 1000 atoms thick) because gold is highly malleable, allowing it to be hammered into ultra thin sheets. A thicker foil would have prevented the α-particles from penetrating. The majority of alpha particles went through the gold foil without any deflection however a smaller number of alpha particles were slightly deflected from their original path. A very few (1 in 8000) were deflected backwards, at angles greater than 90°.

Key Observations and Conclusions:

From the α-particles scattering experiment, Rutherford proposed the following atomic model:

  • (i) An atom has a positively charged centre, called the nucleus, where nearly all the atom's mass is concentrated.
  • (ii) Electrons revolve around the nucleus in circular paths (orbit).
  • (iii) The nucleus is extremely small compared to the overall size of the atom.

Drawbacks of Rutherford's Model

  • The atomic model failed to explain the distribution of electrons around the nucleus and the stability of atoms.
  • It did not explain why atoms emit specific colour when they are heated.
  • It failed to explain why different elements react differently or how electrons are arranged.
  • The atomic model did not include energy levels which was later explained through Bohr's Model (1913).

Artificial Nuclear Reaction (1917)

  • In 1917, Rutherford performed the first artificially induced nuclear reaction

...by conducting experiment in which nitrogen nuclei was bombarded with α-particles.

Key Observations:

  • Rutherford concluded that the hydrogen nucleus is a fundamental particle present in all atoms.
  • He named this positively charged particle the proton (p) in 1920.

Bohr's Model of Atom (1913)

According to this model:

  • Electrons revolve around the nucleus in stable orbits (energy levels or shells) without losing energy in the form of radiation.
  • The orbits or energy levels are labeled K, L, M, N, with K being the closest to the nucleus and N being the farthest.
  • The ground state is the lowest energy level that an electron can occupy, typically referring to the electron's position in the K-shell (the innermost shell).
  • When an electron moves between different energy levels (or shells), it either absorbs or emits energy.
  • When an electron falls from a higher energy level to a lower one, it emits energy, usually in the form of electromagnetic radiation.
  • When an electron moves from a lower energy level to a higher one, it absorbs energy.

Distribution of Electrons (e⁻)

  • The maximum number of e⁻ that can be present in the nth shell is equal to 2n². Thus, we have
  • Last shell/orbit → Valence shell → e⁻ → Valence e⁻
ShellMaximum no. of e⁻
1st shell or K-shell (n = 1)2 × 1² = 2
2nd shell or L-shell (n = 2)2 × 2² = 8
3rd shell or M-shell (n = 3)2 × 3² = 18
4th shell or N-shell (n = 4)2 × 4² = 32

ELECTRON, PROTON, AND NEUTRON

Discovery of Electron, Proton and Neutron

  • Electron discovered by: J. J. Thomson.
  • Proton discovered by: Rutherford or Goldstein.
  • Neutron discovered by: Chadwick (1932).

Comparison of Characteristics of Electron, Proton and Neutron

ParticleCharge on the particleMass of the particleSymbolLocation in the atom
1. Electron-1 unit (-1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulomb)9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg (1/1840 u)⁻₁e⁰Outside the nucleus (Extranuclear part)
2. Proton+1 unit (+1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulomb)1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (1 u)+₁p¹In the nucleus
3. NeutronNo charge1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (1 u)₀n¹In the nucleus
A neutron's mass is approx. 1836 times greater than that of electron.

Neutrons

  • Neutrons are sub-atomic particles that are found in the nucleus of every atom, except for hydrogen, which only has proton in its nucleus.
  • Protons and neutrons are collectively known as nucleons.
  • The mass of neutrons is 1 amu.

Ions

  • The charged species are called Ions.
  • Negative charged ions are Anion.
  • Positive charged ions are Cation.
  • E.g. Sodium Chloride (NaCl) constitutes positively charged Na⁺ (sodium) and negatively charged Cl⁻ (chlorine).
Positron: Discovered in 1932 by Carl Anderson.

Symbols of Elements

  • The symbols of elements were first given by Jacob Berzelius (1813) and were used by Dalton for the first time.
  • He proposed that chemical symbols should be based on the Latin names of the elements.

Atomic Number (Z)

Z = no. of proton (p) = no. of electrons (e⁻)
  • Atomic number is always a whole number, because it represents the total number of protons in an atom.
  • The atomic number of an element does not change during a chemical reaction, as chemical reactions involve only rearrangement of electrons, not changes in the nucleus.
p + n — N (nucleus)

Mass Number (A)

  • Mass number of an element (A) = No. of protons (p) + No. of neutrons (n) (present in the atom of an element).
  • Since protons and neutrons are present in the nucleus, these particles are collectively called nucleons. Thus, Mass number of an element = Number of nucleons in the atom of that element.

Notation: Mass no. (No. of p + n) — a / M / Atomic no. (No. of protons) — Z

  • A = p + n
  • A = Z + n
  • A - Z = n

E.g. Magnesium (Mg):

  • Protons (p⁺) = 12
  • Electrons (e⁻) = 12
  • Neutrons (n₀) = Mass no. — No. of protons = 12

Q. An ion M³⁺ contains 10 electrons and 14 neutrons. What is the mass number and atomic number of element M?

Solution:

  • M³⁺ = 3 e⁻ lost → So originally it had 13 e⁻ → 13 e⁻ = 13 p⁺ = atomic no. = 13
  • A = p + n = 13 + 14 = 27 → Mass no. (A) = No. of protons (p) + No. of neutrons (n)

ISOTOPES

  • Isotopes are atoms of same elements that have same atomic number, but different mass number.
  • Isotope of an element differ only in number of neutrons present in the nucleus.

Isotopes of Hydrogen

  • ¹H (e⁻ = p = 1, n = 0): Protium.
  • ²H (e⁻ = p = 1, n = 1): Deuterium.
  • ³H (e⁻ = p = 1, n = 2): Tritium (radioactive in nature).

Isotopes of Carbon

  • ₆C¹² (e⁻ = p = 6, n = 6): Carbon-12.
  • ₆C¹³ (e⁻ = p = 6, n = 7): Carbon-13.
  • ₆C¹⁴ (e⁻ = p = 6, n = 8): Carbon-14 (used in Carbon Dating to determine age of fossils and rocks).

Characteristics of Isotopes

1. Same Chemical Properties

  • Isotopes have same electronic configuration, hence same number of valance e⁻. Since chemical property depends upon the number of valance e⁻. Therefore, they have same chemical properties.

2. Different Physical Properties

  • Since, the isotopes of an element have different masses, hence different physical properties, like melting point, boiling point, density, etc. exist.

Q. Atomic Mass of Chlorine is 35.5. How?

Solution: ³⁵₁₇Cl : ³⁷₁₇Cl in ratio 3:1, Atomic Mass = (35 × 3 + 37 × 1) / (3 + 1) = 35.5

→ Chlorine has two isotopes Cl-35 and Cl-37 which exists in ratio 3:1.

Uses of Isotopes

  1. 1. In nuclear reactors, isotopes like Uranium-235 are used as fuel to sustain a controlled nuclear chain reaction, generating heat that powers electricity production.
  2. 2. In radiation therapy, isotope Cobalt-60 is used to destroy and prevent cancer cells.
  3. 3. In treatment of goitre, isotope Iodine-131 is used.

ISOBARS

  • Isobars are atoms of different chemical elements that have same mass number, but different atomic numbers.

Isobars and Their Properties

  • They are atoms of different elements.
  • They have different atomic number.
  • They have same mass number.
  • They have similar physical properties and different chemical properties.
  • They have different number of protons, electrons, neutrons.
  • E.g. Argon (Ar), Potassium (K), Calcium (Ca).

Examples: ⁴⁰₁₈Ar (18p, 22n, 18e⁻), ⁴⁰₁₉K (19p, 21n, 19e⁻), ⁴⁰₂₀Ca (20p, 20n, 20e⁻)

ISOTONES

  • Isotones are atoms that have the same neutron number but different proton number.

ATOMICITY

  • Atomicity is the total number of atoms present in a molecule of an element. E.g. Each molecule of Oxygen is composed of two oxygen atoms. Therefore, the atomicity of Oxygen is 2.
ElementAtomicity
ArgonMonoatomic (1)
HeliumMonoatomic
OxygenDiatomic (2)
HydrogenDiatomic
NitrogenDiatomic
ChlorineDiatomic
PhosphorusTetra-atomic (4)
SulphurPoly-atomic

MOLE CONCEPT

Mole

  • It is a unit of measurement that represents the amount of a substance.
  • It is a base unit in the International System of Units (SI).
  • One mole of a substance contains 6.022 × 10²³ elementary entities (Avogadro's Number) such as atoms, molecules, or ions.
No. of Moles = Given Mass (m) / Molecular Mass (M) = Given no. of Particles (N) / Avogadro No. (N₀) → N = m/M = N/N₀

E.g. Copper: 6.022 × 10²³ atoms — Avogadro's No.; 1 mole of Cu = 63.5 g; 1 mole of Cu = 63.5 g

Q. What will be the number of moles in 2g of Helium (He)?

Solution: n = 2/4 = 1/2 = 0.5 moles

→ The molecular mass of helium = 2 + 2 = 4 (2 → protons, 2 → neutrons)

Q. What will be the number of moles in 12.044 × 10²² particles of N atoms?

Solution: n = (12.044 × 10²²) / (6.022 × 10²³) = 20/100 = 0.2 moles
